#2038. Championship data highlights exactly what West Ham’s midfield is still missing

A fascinating piece of Championship analysis from Loft Insights on X may provide an uncomfortable reminder of where West Ham’s midfield falls short.

The graphic plots central midfielders based on two key metrics: line-breaking passes per 90 minutes and ball-winning actions per 90 minutes. Put simply, it measures which players are able to progress the ball through opposition lines while also contributing defensively.

The most interesting takeaway for me was not necessarily which players stand out, but where West Ham’s own midfield profiles sit on the chart.

The Championship’s elite midfielders increasingly occupy the top-right quadrant, combining progression and defensive intensity. That is why the chart identifies Norwich City’s Kenny McLean as one of the Championship’s most complete midfielders, posting outstanding line-breaking numbers while maintaining strong defensive output, despite only featuring for ten games out of fifteen due to an ankle injury.

Meanwhile, Portsmouth’s Ebou Adams is highlighted as a “defensive monster”, producing exceptional ball-winning statistics while still offering significant progression. Sheffield United’s Kalvin Phillips (yes the same player that flopped on loan at West Ham!), Queens Park Rangers’ Jonathan Varane and Norwich’s Jacob Wright also occupy impressive positions, demonstrating the ability to impact both sides of the game.

Mohamadou Kanté is viewed as a dynamic ball-carrying midfielder with strong physical attributes, but his game is built more around energy and transition play than elite progression metrics. Arne Engels offers technical quality and creativity, yet is generally more comfortable operating higher up the pitch than acting as a defensive controller.

The data is only based on players who have played an average of 540 mins so one omission is Tomas Souček, whose strengths have always been obvious. The Czech international on paper would arguably be the Championships most effective midfield goalscorer (3 in 7 appearances so far) and I’d expect him to feature highly for aerial presence. However, if plotted on a graph measuring line-breaking passes and ball-winning volume, he would likely owe more to his physicality and attacking threat than his ability to dictate possession through midfield.

That perhaps explains why West Ham can sometimes appear disconnected between defence and attack.

Too often there is a reliance on direct balls into attacking areas rather than building through the centre of the pitch. Equally, when possession is lost, the midfield does not always possess the combination of mobility and defensive output needed to regain control quickly.

West Ham arguably have midfielders who can create and win duels. What they appear to lack is a genuine “two-way” midfielder capable of consistently ranking highly in both categories.

That was precisely what Declan Rice offered during his time at the club. His ability to recover possession and immediately progress the ball remains incredibly difficult to replace.

The reality is Rice was never truly replaced, although finding a like-for-like successor was always going to be a near-impossible task

Former West Ham midfielder James Ward-Prowse’s position on the chart is also interesting. A casualty of Nuno’s reign, he ranks among the highest players for line-breaking passes but has one of the lowest ball-winning outputs. Ward-Prowse excels at progressing possession but offers relatively little defensive contribution compared to the league’s most complete midfielders.

Above all the data serves as a reminder that Koppen’s recruitment and Parker’s existing choices for midfield should focus less on individual statistics and more on complete profiles.

Because the numbers suggest that is where Championship matches are increasingly won.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

I think there is nothing wrong with the Midfield. There is just a problem with the short pass mentality. The day of playing short passes across midfield are over in English football. You need decent long passes with good trapping and decent positive movement. How many of West Ham’s passes are square ball or back passes ? Far to many. Particularly back passes are all to often caught on to giving away needless goals. Walker-Peters is a really good example. Having moved forward beating someone, he then passes back in midfield, or worst still carries the ball backwards towards midfield or defence. Play positively, avoid back passes, learn to pass well and trap well and you have a very good midfield. Orford, Kante and other young players are far better at doing this, than the older players.

#2037. Andy Burnham and his comments on the 3pm Saturday blackout got me thinking

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The headline declared that Andy Burnham has urged caution on scrapping the 3pm Saturday TV blackout.

Ahead of this latest international break I was at the Fulham v Newcastle United game, the novelty of it being a rare 3pm kick-off for NUFC.

The BBC article that I was reading, stated: “The blackout originated in the 1960s when Burnley chairman Bob Lord encouraged the EFL to oppose television coverage of 3pm Saturday matches.”

I understand the sentiments expressed by Andy Burnham, as he doesn’t want to be seen as upsetting the lower league clubs who are dependent on match day receipts and the peripheral spending.

However, when you look at the amount of games in the Premier League played outside the Saturday 3pm kick-off, you begin to wonder.

The working man’s game where you could rock up to St James’ Park with a belly full of ale for a 3pm kick-off and pay at the turnstiles are a thing of the past and long gone.

Take a look at the Newcastle United fixtures so far this season and you will see Fulham really was novelty.

In these first five months of the 2026-27 Premier League season only three 3pm Saturday kick-offs for Newcastle United, home to Hull and away to Fulham, plus Ipswich away next month.

All of these Premier League games played outside of the 3pm Saturday slot is a boon for lower league clubs. Due to technology, I can watch Newcastle play at 3pm on a Saturday even when I don’t get a ticket for the match.

But the 3pm Saturday kick-off is such a rarity it has become an irrelevance.

As the Newcastle United games are now shown at an increasingly ridiculous range of times, that frees up Saturday afternoon for me and my mates to go down to Dulwich Hamlet on a Saturday afternoon and have a pint of Peckham pale ale on the terracing while watching live football in the Isthmian Premier League.

So as me and my lad fail to get home tickets for Newcastle United on a regular basis now (no need for tiny violins), we are down the Hamlet on a Saturday afternoon with hundreds of other like minded Premier League team supporting people, who simply want to see live football kicking off at a proper time.

#2036. How Liverpool feel about January recall for Ifeanyi Ndukwe amid Premier League loan enquiries

Liverpool are reportedly keen for Ifeanyi Ndukwe to continue his development on loan with Levante in Spain, despite the player now being eligible for a UK work permit.

The 18-year-old was a revelation for the Reds in pre-season but, at the time, he didn’t meet the criteria to play competitively in England and was subsequently dispatched to the LaLiga outfit for this season.

He’s continued to perform impressively for Los Azulgranas, and there were reports last month of his agents arranging to discuss the possibility of a January recall to Anfield.

According to Graeme Bailey for TEAMtalk, Liverpool are convinced that Ndukwe could break into their first-team setup next year and view him as ‘hugely important’ for their long-term plans.

Although he could theoretically be recalled in January, the Reds’ preference is for him to remain with Levante for the rest of his season and proceed with his development there.

That hasn’t stopped some Premier League clubs from enquiring about his availability for a loan move for the second half of the campaign to give him a first taste of English top-flight football.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Having had to wait until October for his first start for Levante, Ndukwe was then included from the first whistle in all six of their LaLiga games since the extended international break earlier in the autumn (Transfermarkt).

Luis Castro demonstrably has faith in the Austrian teenager, whose performances on loan have earned praise from the Spanish media, although the occasional error has served as a reminder that he’s still developing and will have off-days as part of that.

While Premier League exposure would be a quite informative barometer of the youngster’s readiness for the Liverpool first team, we’d be in favour of him continuing with Levante if he’s enjoying regular game-time there.

At the moment Ndukwe is featuring regularly in one of Europe’s foremost domestic leagues, and doing so with a club where media attention and scrutiny is comparatively sparse, thus keeping him away from the harshest of exposure.

He must be doing plenty right to have English top-flight clubs asking about taking him on loan in the winter. If that’s the case, then the current plan seems to be working, and we see no reason to deviate from that any time soon.

#2034. Incredible story as Newcastle United teenager creates history with Brazil

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Newcastle United teenager Matheos Ferreira has made history in the colours of Brazil.

The exciting 18-year-old winger got his first ever call up for his country this month.

Matheos Ferreira named in the Brazil Under 20s squad for a double header with Peru.

He was an unused sub on Friday when the young Brazil stars won 2-0.

Then on Monday he made history, Matheos Ferreira becoming the first player developed at the Newcastle United Academy to go on to represent Brazil at international level.

The 18-year-old is from Berwick but is eligible to represent the country through his Brazilian father, Thiago.

Not only did Matheos Ferreira make his first ever start for the Brazil Under 20s on Monday, it only took him 14 minutes to score!

The United winger putting Brazil into the lead against Peru Under 20s in Belem.

— Bradley Robson (@bradrobson2605) November 17, 2026

Matheos Ferreira seeing his dream international debut get even better when he also supplied an assist as the Brazil youngsters routed the opposition and won 9-0 against Peru.

The Newcastle United Academy star talked to official NUFC club media from Brazil ahead of his debut: “I had to start training as soon as I got there but I think it’s shown how far I have come as a player because I wasn’t too nervous or anxious… I am doing the thing I love the most, playing football, and it was nice to get on the pitch and train with the squad. It’s been busy! The culture is completely different here but I really like it. We’re having to train in the evening as it is usually over 30 degrees during the day. Since the first training session, I’ve felt very welcome by the lads and the coaches as well.”

Matheos Ferreira also qualifies to play potentially for England and Italy (his mam’s Italian).

The winger joined the Newcastle United Academy in 2020 after playing for Berwick Juniors and Cramlington Juniors and recalled the moment he found out he’d got his first Brazil call up: “My first reaction was just pure joy. I was so happy. My parents wanted to tell me first before I checked my phone but it was still a great moment to share with them, who were both very emotional. I think it’s a reward for how I’ve been playing but also how I’ve managed to conduct myself off the pitch with my recovery, willingness to learn and reflecting on how I can improve on the matches I’ve played in. It’s an amazing achievement but I don’t want this to be the last. I will keep pushing on and try to get that next call-up or progress into the first-team. Once I reach one level, it’s about getting to the next one. It doesn’t stop there. We’ve got the South American (Youth Football) Championship in January and the Under-20 World Cup is next year so I’m pushing really hard to try and get into both squads. I’m doing everything I can to try and make my international debut. It would mean a lot. I haven’t got this big pressure of needing to do well – I just want to get on that pitch, show what I can do and do what I love the most.”

Matheos Ferreira remembering: “My first memory of Brazilian football would be my dad showing videos of Ronaldinho, R9 and Neymar,” he added. “The first game I watched live was at Wembley between England and Brazil and Neymar played. I think it finished goalless though! The interest they showed me and the project they have was a big reason [to accept the call-up]. Brazil is a big country so to be recognised by them is amazing. It’s a big opportunity and an honour to represent them.”

The 18-year-old rising Newcastle United star is buzzing with how the 2026-27 season has kicked off, for club and country: “I’ve really enjoyed the start to this season. The coaches trust me as I’ve been playing in different positions for the Under-21s; wing-back, as a winger or a number ten. I think they know what I can provide for the team. I think its shows the qualities I have. Playing as a right wing-back shows I can defend, put my body on the line and then it’s about showing my strengths going forward. I’ve embraced the challenges of switching positions, thinking about the tactical side of the game.”

A brilliant moment on Monday for Matheos Ferreira and here’s to many more appearances (and goals!) in the colours of Brazil AND Newcastle United.

The Mag Podcast Episode 17: Newcastle United’s 2015-16 relegation with lessons from the past

Published: 16/11/2026 | Duration: 46 mins | Hosts: Jamie Smith, Simon Cahill & David Hutchinson

In Episode 17 of The Mag Pod, we find Jamie, Simon, and Hutch discussing relegation, again! Special focus is on the 2015-16 season when the combined talents of Mike Ashley and Steve McClaren led to the club’s most recent drop to the Championship. So how does the current 2026-27 NUFC situation compare…?

You can play episode 17 on the audio player above or use your favourite podcast platforms including Spotify, Apple Podcasts, Amazon Music, YouTube, and Acast.

Listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! Join Jamie, Simon, and Hutch for unfiltered football debate.

Jamie Smith, Simon Cahill and David Hutchinson revisit Newcastle United’s 2015-16 relegation season under the ownership of Mike Ashley, examining the failures under Steve McClaren, the arrival of Rafa Benítez and whether there are lessons to be learned amid the concerns surrounding the current 2026-27 campaign.

The lads also discuss Newcastle United Women’s derby draw with Sunderland and the controversial travel restrictions for the upcoming Tyne-Wear derby.

In the second of three episodes this week, Hutch takes us through another particularly forgettable chapter in Newcastle United’s history. From a disappointing start to the season and a recruitment policy that prioritised potential over experience, to a divided dressing room and a lack of leadership on the pitch, there was no shortage of contributing factors to United’s downfall.

There’s a look back at the performances of Georginio Wijnaldum, Aleksandar Mitrović, Fabricio Coloccini and Moussa Sissoko, as well as some personal memories of the campaign, including a frustrating afternoon at Old Trafford and a particularly miserable pre-Christmas encounter with Aston Villa.

Could an earlier appointment of Rafa Benítez have saved Newcastle from relegation?

The lads discuss the importance of knowing when to make a managerial change, whilst considering the differences between the Newcastle United of a decade ago and the club today.

There’s also an assessment of the increasingly congested Premier League table, the importance of experienced players in a transitional squad and the heroes and villains of the 2015-16 season.

Naturally, a controversial Sergio Agüero goal brings about another argument between Jamie and Simon over the merits of VAR, with all the maturity listeners have come to expect.

Another nostalgic look at a period Newcastle United fans would rather forget, but one which offers plenty of talking points given the challenges facing United today.

#2031. Jacob Murphy is not our future but he IS the here and now

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

In the grand and often unforgiving theatre of Premier League football, where stars are minted in bursts of brilliance and extinguished by the next transfer window, there are players whose value is measured not solely in highlight reels but in the quiet accumulation of purpose.

Jacob Murphy belongs to that rarer company.

At 31, the Newcastle United winger continues to embody a particular kind of professional resilience—one forged in loans, tempered by reinvention, and now expressed in moments that still make the away end rise as one.

I know, we’ve heard the complaints of many fans and pundits that Jacob Murphy is “not good enough”, that he disappears for long stretches during the match, that we need an upgrade at the position. Maybe. The lad is not perfect or to everyone’s liking but he is my cup of tea. He produces with first-time crosses into the box, always gives 100%, readily gets back on defence, and adds a bit of needed comic relief.

Born in Wembley on 24 February 1995 to parents with roots in NE England, Murphy carried Newcastle in his blood long before he wore the shirt. A boyhood Magpie who grew up visiting family in Gateshead, he and his twin brother Josh cut their teeth at Norwich City’s academy. Together they helped win the FA Youth Cup in 2013. Jacob’s path thereafter was the classic English apprenticeship of the lower leagues: temporary homes at Swindon, Southend, Blackpool, Scunthorpe, Colchester, and, most formatively, a season-long stay at Coventry City in 2015-16 where he scored ten goals and announced himself as a player of genuine threat. Returning to Norwich, he produced a breakthrough campaign of nearly double figures in goals and assists, enough to persuade Rafa Benítez to bring him to St James’ Park in the summer of 2017 for a fee in the region of £12 million.

The early years on Tyneside were not seamless. There were loans—to West Bromwich Albion and Sheffield Wednesday—and the familiar struggle of a young wide player trying to impose himself in a club that was itself searching for direction (certainly, Steve Bruce was not the man to coach him up).

What changed everything was the arrival of Eddie Howe.

Under Howe, Jacob Murphy was transformed from squad option into indispensable operator. He became the energetic wide presence who pressed, crossed, tracked, and, with increasing frequency, delivered. The 2024-25 season marked his high-water mark: eight Premier League goals and a dozen assists, a body of work that placed him among the league’s most productive creators from the flank. He scored in the Carabao Cup semi-final against Arsenal and provided a decisive assist in the final as Newcastle United ended a 70-year wait for a major domestic trophy. For a player once dismissed by some as a useful squad man, it was validation of the highest order.

Murphy’s assets have never been those of the purest technician or the most glamorous dribbler. He is direct. He is tireless. He possesses a left foot capable of bending a ball from distance with sudden, almost unfair venom, and a right foot that can pick out a player in the box. Was Alexander Isak worth the money Liverpool paid without the assists of Murphy? I’d argue that we got top money from the Reds for the rat – and Murphy’s crosses were a major contributor. His willingness to occupy the spaces that make others look better. He crosses with purpose, contributes defensively without complaint, and brings a structural intelligence that managers prize.

In a squad that has undergone significant change—younger faces arriving, senior voices departing—his experience has become a form of quiet leadership. Even after being omitted from the formal player leadership group under new head coach Matthias Jaissle, Murphy has spoken of an unchanged responsibility: to add value, to set standards, to help the younger players understand what the Premier League demands week after week.

This season has been more measured than the explosion of 2024-25. Minutes have been shared; the goal tally has been slower to climb. Yet the importance remains as he’s more dependable than Anthony Elanga and much more experienced that Matias Fernandez-Pardo.

On a November afternoon at Craven Cottage, with Newcastle searching for a response after consecutive defeats, Murphy produced the kind of moment that defines him. Intercepting a loose pass, he drove forward, cut inside, and from fully 25 yards unleashed a curling left-footed strike that left Bernd Leno helpless. The goal was his first of the campaign. It was also a reminder.

Three minutes later Fulham equalised (of course they did) but the point was earned in part because of that individual quality and the industry that preceded it. Days earlier he had provided an assist in a clean-sheet victory at Crystal Palace. The pattern is familiar: when Newcastle need a spark or a measure of control on the flank, Murphy is often the player trusted to provide it.

There is something almost old-fashioned in his story. In an era of astronomical fees and instantaneous celebrity, Murphy has built a career through persistence, adaptation, and an unshowy professionalism. He has scored against Manchester City in his early days, netted a brace against Tottenham (including a scorcher!), contributed to European nights and a first major trophy in generations. He has survived the doubts that accompany any player who does not fit the neatest marketing narrative. Now, with his contract situation under discussion and interest from elsewhere already rejected by the club, he continues to state the obvious with clarity: he knows what he brings.

I am not advocating that Jacob Murphy is our future but he IS the here and now. The best we have at his position and, until we can get in a player with better talent and upside, indispensable for the team this season.

For Newcastle United in this transitional season under Jaissle, that contribution—energy, experience, the capacity for the sudden decisive strike—remains quietly essential. Jacob Murphy does not demand the spotlight. He simply continues to occupy the spaces where the game is still won, one determined run, one precise cross, one unforgettable curler at a time.

In the long narrative of a club that has known both glory and patience, his is a chapter written in steady ink. I think its time to give him some respect. 🎙️ THE MAG PODCAST Ep 15: Fulham frustration, Newcastle United’s season report card and Relegation fears Listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! Having watched some of Tottenham’s signings fall to a 3-0 Premier League defeat by Brentford a few days earlier, Sávio’s late impact was the perfect lift for the Spurs supporters.

The club have committed to spending almost £400m this summer, leading to debate by outsiders over whether it will prove to be money well spent and huge waves of excitement within the fanbase.

A deal that could be worth as much as £85m, if add-ons are achieved, for Sávio certainly raised some eyebrows, but the Brazilian provided the perfect response by scoring just 11 minutes into his debut as a late substitute.

In the 82nd minute, Sávio cut in from the flank and scored with a shot past Charlton goalkeeper Tiernan Brooks. He and the Spurs crowd thought he had a second a few minutes later, but his shot hit Ben Davies on its way into the net and the defender was credited with the goal.

Having sung for Moore earlier in the game, the Spurs fans wasted no time in trying out their new song for Sávio, inspired by the Spandau Ballet hit Gold.

Moore has been expected to move to Cologne on loan, but provided a reminder of his talent by opening the scoring in the first half with only his second goal for the club.

What a hit from Mikey Moore! ⚪ pic.twitter.com/OgSM4qhiqs

“We have to understand the best solution,” De Zerbi said. “I would like to keep him. He’s young but a good player, but we can’t make the wrong decision. He needs to play, he needs to get games inside him.”

Cutting in from the right, where Sávio is primed to play, Moore surged past his marker and shot from just inside the box. Brooks should have stopped it, but the ball flew past him and into the net.

Three minutes after Moore’s opener, Dominic Solanke scored his first goal since March to offer a reminder of what he can still give De Zerbi, who is poised to welcome Omar Marmoush to Tottenham.

Buoyed by his first-half goal, Moore skipped his way around a couple of tackles at the start of the second period but his low cross was cut out. The Spurs fans responded by singing “he’s one of our own.”

Substitute Kevin Danso netted with his first touch from a header, before Sávio was introduced to steal the show, despite a late consolation goal from Charlton’s Lloyd Jones.

Kevin Danso scores with his first touch since coming on! ⚪ pic.twitter.com/oqUU7wjoJW

The victory set up a tough third-round trip to Anfield to face Liverpool for Tottenham, but De Zerbi said: “It’s a great game. If we want to win the competition we have to win the games.

“Sometimes in this competition, it can happen that you play against big teams. It’s a great challenge for the players, for me, for our clubs. We have to arrive ready to play in our style, with personality, ready to play a game following the work we are doing on the training ground.”

A place in the League Cup third round is at stake as Tottenham host Charlton in a London derby at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. The last competitive meeting between these sides came in the FA Cup back in January 2011, with Tottenham winning that game 3-0 at White Hart Lane. A then 19-year-old Andros Townsend made his debut that day and scored, with Jermain Defoe scoring a brace.

Tottenham’s Premier League campaign got off to the worst possible start as they lost 3-0 at Brentford last weekend. Tottenham have been very busy during this summer transfer window and that has continued this week. Savio (formerly Savinho) has arrived from Manchester City in a deal that could be worth £85m and the Brazilian could make his Tottenham debut tonight, having been registered in time.

“I think in attacking positions we need players capable one-on one, to create something, to create a chance to score,” Roberto De Zerbi said. “In terms of one-on-one, he [Savio] is one of the best players, especially since 2024. He can play on the right side, on the left side. I have known him from a long time, I spoke with him when he went to Manchester City. He is a big player for us.

“I do not know if I am the right man [to get the most out of Savio], but for sure he has to achieve. I think a player who is so good in one-on-one, so good at creating chances to score, to be complete, he has to score. If you analyse the other best wingers in the world, many of them, they score 10 to 15 goals per season. He has the qualities. Maybe his habits, he has to change habits, because he has to be focused on the assists, the one-on-one dribbling and also to score.”

Omar Marmoush is closing in on an initial loan deal from Manchester City but that move is not complete and thus he is not available for Tottenham tonight. Micky van der Ven and Pedro Porro are both available having missed Tottenham’s loss at Brentford but the hosts are still without Xavi Simons, Pape Sarr, Dejan Kulusevski and Wilson Odobert.

Charlton have made the perfect start to their Championship campaign; a 2-1 home win over Derby was followed up by a 2-1 victory at recently-relegated West Ham. Nathan Jones’ side earned their place in the League Cup second round with a 3-1 win at Cheltenham in the first round.

“We have to be very organised and very professional, they [Tottenham] are a top team,” Jones said. “They have a great manager and a brilliant group of players. They already had a Premier League squad and they have spent, what is reaching about, I do not know, £300 million or something like that. It is a wonderful test, we have to be right near our best and do both sides of the game very well. Of course, you want to test yourself against the best managers and you want to test yourself against the best teams. For us, this is not our priority, the Championship is our priority, but this is the next game and therefore it is the most important.”

#2029. ‘They had different ideas’ – Rafa Benitez opens up about ‘difficult’ Hicks and Gillett era at LFC

Rafael Benitez has opened up about the ‘difficult’ time that he had at Liverpool during the damaging ownership era of Tom Hicks and George Gillett.

The American businessmen bought the Merseyside club in 2007 amid grandiose promises about a new stadium in Stanley Park (‘a spade in the ground within 60 days’, and all that), but they quickly became hugely unpopular figures among the fan base.

As the duo ultimately fell out with one another amid a period of civil war at the club, debts mounted to the extent that LFC was on the brink of administration in 2010 before they were ousted by a takeover from New England Sports Ventures (now Fenway Sports Group).

In an interview with The Athletic, Benitez was asked if he ever thought back to what could’ve been for Liverpool had it not been for the damaging ownership of Hicks and Gillett, throughout which time the Spaniard kept the club challenging for major silverware.

The former Reds boss reflected: “Yes, 100%. When Hicks and Gillett came, they changed the approach. All the things you did for the benefit of the club, they had different ideas. I realised, and the fans realised later, that something was wrong. They didn’t have experience of football.

“I remember speaking to Gillett once in London after we played Tottenham. He said: ‘We will give you money and then next season you’ll get us into the play-offs.’ I had to tell him there were no play-offs.

“They thought maybe: ‘Rafa is a threat.’ That period was difficult, but all I ever wanted was the best for the club.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Benitez’s final season at Liverpool in 2009/10 was a major disappointment, with the Reds expected to challenge for the title but slumping to a seventh-place finish, and there was a prevailing sentiment that the time was right for a change in the dugout.

However, as the extent of the damage done by Hicks and Gillett became clear in subsequent months and years, the latter part of the Spaniard’s managerial reign has come to be viewed in a much kinder light.

He was left with an impossible job of trying to achieve success on the pitch while all sorts of strife was going on in the background, slowly eating away at the club until John Henry rode to the rescue in October 2010.

Benitez’s time at Liverpool may have ended on a low ebb, but he remains a greatly appreciated figure among the fans for delivering Champions League glory in Istanbul and getting the Reds back to being a competitive force domestically and on the continent, even if the Premier League eluded him.

Had it not been for the incompetence of those at ownership level, who knows just how much more the Spaniard could’ve achieved at Anfield in the late 2000s and possibly into the 2010s?

#2028. 9 rule changes to help the referee cut out cheating and make the game fairer

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The referee and his role in what’s wrong with football.

One of the many problems with football in England is the refereeing.

Not necessarily the refs themselves, more the ever-changing guidance and policies they are expected to obey when it comes to their refereeing.

The Premier League is the world’s most popular, watched all around the globe on television in far higher numbers than any other rival.

It is a money-spinning product that cannot afford to lose its pre-eminent position. Those in charge, such as Richard Masters, the Premier League’s chief executive, have millions of reasons to protect the brand.

In his particular case, 2.6 million for the financial year ending on July 31, 2025. That included a £1.1m bonus awarded in part for his help in negotiating record-breaking broadcasting deals with Sky, TNT and Amazon.

That £2.6m remuneration package (as they like to say in the City of London) was £700,000 up on the previous year. Don’t expect any reduction when the 2025-26 figures are lodged at Companies House . . .

The Premier League’s popularity relies on more than having some of the world’s best players. It also depends on the characteristic style of play being distinctly different from La Liga or the Bundesliga or Serie A. Which is where the refereeing comes in.

You might believe a referee’s primary role is to ensure, to the best of his ability, the game is played fairly. You might be right, though I suspect the job of protecting the brand has become the driving force for the man in the middle and his colleagues.

The more free kicks, the less attractive the spectacle. Those in charge of the Premier League cannot afford a stop-start product, because viewer figures are paramount.

Pro Ref knows this, the players know this, the managers know this. That’s why so many fouls go unpunished. Not because the referees should go to Specsavers. They see them and choose to ignore them.

It’s the coward’s way. Or should that be Howard’s Way? Mr Webb, the head of Pro Ref, was pilloried when VAR kept halting the action. He responded by telling the boys and girls at Stockley Park to intervene in only the most extreme cases.

Outcome: a non-decision by the ref is not corrected by the VAR.

The most blatant mistakes are later scrutinised by the Premier League’s key match incidents panel. Its verdicts read like an Orwellian nightmare.

In a typical case, a penalty is not awarded for foul play. The VAR, obeying Howard’s Way, looks and agrees. Days later, the key match incidents panel says: “A penalty was probably the right call but VAR was correct in doing nothing. If the ref had blown for the foul, the VAR would have agreed.”

So there you have it. Whichever call the referee makes is correct. It must be, because the VAR backed him up. Reminds me of the olden days when the referee’s decision was final.

Before each season starts, changes are announced to the way the laws of the game will be enforced. Among recent initiatives was the five-second countdown on throws and goal kicks if the referee detected time wasting. They are rarely enforced because the threat of being penalised has encouraged quicker play, as intended. There’s also a 10-second limit for a substituted player to leave the field.

Nobody would argue against those changes, though they smack of window dressing when much more important problems are being ignored. Here are just a few suggestions to make the game fairer.

1. Warn any player who refuses to retreat 10 yards promptly from an opponent’s free kick. The second time he or a teammate does it, book the offender. Third time, red card.

2. Issue a yellow card for pushing whenever no attempt is made to play the ball.

3. Award a throw-in to the other team if the ball is not released from behind the head. Or if both feet are not grounded behind the touchline. Or if the throw is taken more than two yards forward of the right point. Players know.

4) Book any player who pulls an opponent’s shirt, shorts or socks.

5) Stop players taking free kicks from the wrong spot. If they do it again, book them. Keepers in particular move the ball up the field or towards their goal with impunity, knowing the referee will do nothing.

6) A yellow card for all offences of dissent, either physical or verbal, directed at the referee or his assistants. Including the captain.

7) An automatic card to any player who dives. In the opponents’ penalty area, make it a red.

8) Add on at least one minute for every goal celebration.

9) Play an advantage if there is the chance of one but go back and book any player who has fouled off the ball.

You might think there would be a blizzard of yellow and red cards. I believe the far more likely consequence would be a massive reduction in gamesmanship, cheating, time wasting and other examples of the dark arts that are blighting the beautiful game.

Once players realised they couldn’t foul with impunity, they would quickly learn to play the game as a sport, rather than as a cynical win-at-all-costs exercise.

#2027. West Ham Winger Faces Another Fitness Test As Parker Waits

West Ham United are facing something of a dilemma over Manor Solomon, with Israel reportedly considering bringing the winger back into the team for Tuesday’s Nations League clash against Austria. The 26-year-old has been struggling with back pain during the international break, although Israel manager Ran Ben-Shimon has suggested that he is feeling better after returning to training.

According to Sport5, Solomon could now be in contention for the Austria fixture. That follows comments from Ben-Shimon suggesting the player had trained and was feeling better, although his fitness would need to be reassessed.

For West Ham manager Scott Parker, however, the situation presents an interesting dilemma. We desperately need the old Manor Solomon back, but I wonder whether another international appearance is really what the player needs right now.

Manor Solomon representing Israel during a difficult international break. The West Ham winger has been carrying a back injury since October

Look, I’m caught between a rock and a hard place on this one.

There is part of me that hopes Solomon gets a game, so he can get back to form. Because there’s no doubt about it, West Ham have a far bigger chance of getting promoted this season if Manor Solomon is back to the sort of form he was in when he played for Leeds in the Championship.

Clearly Scott Parker has faith in him because he has seen how destructive he can be in that division. Getting that player back would be a significant boost for the Hammers, particularly with the Championship promotion race starting to get serious.

But, and it’s a big but, we have had complaints of back injury during the October internationals, and we’ve already had it during this international break.

As I reported earlier in October, a West Ham source confirmed that Solomon was in considerable pain after an exhausting international schedule. More recently, we reported on his latest back problem, which restricted his training with Israel.

There is also part of me that wonders whether we would not have been better served, and the player himself, actually resting up, getting some medical treatment, or even being given ten days off completely to recuperate and joining back up with the squad for the last few days of training before the Preston game.

As things stand, there’s nothing in his recent form that suggests he could start and should start against Preston. And without him being on the training pitch during this international break to impress Scott Parker, he’s not going to be able to catch the manager’s eye.

Edvin Austbø has certainly given Parker something to think about on the left wing. Indeed, Austbø’s recent performances have highlighted the competition for Solomon’s place, and I suspect the Norwegian is currently ahead of him in the pecking order.

But I don’t want to write off Solomon. We know what he’s capable of producing in this division, and West Ham will need every bit of attacking quality available if we’re serious about getting back into the Premier League.

Hopefully, Israel will make the sensible decision and only involve him against Austria if he is genuinely fit enough to play. We cannot afford another international break to leave us with a player who returns to east London carrying another injury.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

With over a decade of professional sports media experience, he is a frequent West Ham United analyst and contributor for Sky Sports News, BBC Football Focus, and BBC Radio 5 Live. He previously served as an official video and content creator for West Ham United FC during the club's tenure at Upton Park and featured in the official documentary commemorating the historic final game at the Boleyn Ground.

A lifelong Hammer since the legendary 10-0 victory over Bury, when he isn't providing daily match analysis on the Hammers Chat YouTube Channel or broadcasting on X (@GONZObignose), he can be found walking his dog and restoring classic pinball machines.

If Solomon does play Tuesday it’s not exactly a gentle one. Israel are bottom of Nations League B Group 3 with 3 points from 5 (0 wins, 3 draws, 2 defeats, goal difference -5) and Austria top it unbeaten on 11. On those numbers it looks more like a damage-limitation night than one to rebuild form in. (Figures from the PickGround match page, posting as the PickGround team, free prediction site.) #2026. The Mike Ashley relegations pre Newcastle United takeover and lessons to be learnt

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

I hold my hands up that I was guilty of a bit of an oversight during The Mag Podcast last week.

“Those who do not learn from the past are doomed to repeat it” – George Santayana

I half remembered the quote above and threw it to my co-host Hutch on The Mag Pod to try and recite it verbatim, as he likes history and stuff like that.

There were two errors involved to be fair, me for putting him on the spot like that, and Hutch for being as thick as mince.

Jamie puts Hutch on the spot over Newcastle United’s relegation history

Anyway, I’ve since found the appropriate wording and replicated as a starting point here, as a way of conveying what we’ve been doing on The Mag Pod as we tried to fill the ongoing international break. Basically, there has been some chatter and paranoia that the issues this Newcastle United side are facing this season could well lead to a relegation battle. If it does turn out that way, it won’t be any of our first rodeos.

However, it’s fair to say that many of those Mike Ashley era struggles ended fairly benignly, with the drop avoided. On occasions this was comfortably, at times it was squeaky, but it didn’t really matter as long as you lived to fight another day. Unfortunately, there were exceptions.

So, to try and learn the lessons of history, we have used this round of podcasts to look at the Mike Ashley seasons where it went terribly wrong.

Late last week the first instalment (Episode 16) dropped, as we took a walk through the chaotic 2008-09 season. The follow-up, reliving the relegation of 2015-16 (Episode 17), which is out now.

These serve as both a wander through times gone by and a study in what we can learn.

Ideally, listeners may feel better about current circumstances in comparison with the poor decisions, awful form and careless business that led to highly avoidable seasons away from the Premier League under the previous regime.

Unfortunately there may be times when certain things ring true and we appear in real danger of breaking Mr Santayana’s above rule.

There is a third instalment to come as well, but alas we are a bit wet behind the lugs to fully recount the demotion of 1988-89.

Instead, a slight change of tack is incoming where Thursday’s edition (Episode 18) will see a review of the 2020-21 season, the final year before the Newcastle United takeover. This is to give a perspective on how far we have come, the impact of the considerable changes since and to hopefully make you all feel better you’re no longer looking at Steve Bruce.

Spoiler alert, but the general overall conclusion of these editions is that more time and consideration is needed in the current circumstances, to really have a full and proper idea of how badly it may compare to some of our darker times. However, there are things in there that may very well resonate.

Please enjoy The Mag Podcast and we’d love your feedback on what we have done so far and suggestions for the future in the commenting section below.

#2025. Now entering the debate on whether Bruno Guimaraes is returning Toon hero or Toon turncoat

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

I have been reading lately, with interest, the conversations surrounding the return of Bruno Guimaraes to St James’ Park this coming weekend (Saturday 21st November)

Opinion seems to be split as to what kind of reception our former captain should receive if he is selected to face us on Saturday evening.

Since leaving Newcastle United, Bruno Guimaraes hasn’t been an automatic starter, so we may not have the chance to show him our collective feelings either way.

From what I am reading the camp seems to be split directly down the middle between “Bruno Guimaraes is a hero who led us to our first silverware in decades”, to “Bruno Guimaraes is a traitor who went all out to manufacture a move away from the club.”

Looking back now at the summer dealings it’s easier to reflect on what happened and why the players who left, did.

In my opinion , it was only a matter of time before Sandro left us, his heart never seemed in the Northeast, neither does it in North London to be honest, the only time I think we will see him truly happy is when he is plying his trade back in Italy, unfortunately for him it doesn’t look as if Italian football could subsidise that kind of financial arrangement.

Again, in my opinion the same can be said about Anthony Gordon, I liked the lad but also got the impression he thought he was destined for a bigger club, something which was proven to be true.

I just got the impression he thought he was too big a name for the club and it was a matter of time before he left. The fact he went abroad seemed to make the move slightly more palatable as a Newcastle fan.

And on to Bruno, I love(d) the bloke, I was stood in the away section of the Stadium of light, with 7,000 others, 3-0 up and watched him slide tackle on our own goal line and celebrate as if he had scored.

I loved his passion and enthusiasm for the game and the Toon. He could drive and win a game single handedly by grabbing the team by the scruff of the neck and pushing the team forward.

I loved his speech at the Town Moor presentation and the way he appreciated the character of the Northeast.

Will I boo him if he plays on Saturday? 100%. This is not out of spite; I take this decision more so on a few factors.

Bruno Guimaraes is a confidence player; we have seen this ourselves over the years. We know he feels bad about leaving, he has made a few statements leading up to the game about the toughest decision he has had to make-blah blah blah etc.

But, he went out of his way to hire a super-agent in Kia Joorabchian to help get a move away. Not the actions of a player in love with the glorious Northeast.

He had opportunities to soften the blow of leaving many times over the course of the 2026 World Cup but chose the coward’s way out with total silence, despite the obvious effect it would have on the fans

Let’s get at him, rattle him, affect his confidence, and take the roof off every time Dan Burn cuts him in half, maybe that will be enough to unsettle him and his teammates.

Newcastle United are in a transitional period as a team, but I still feel on a Saturday evening kick off, with a crowd fuelled with day drinking we can beat anyone..

Maybe spare applause for Bruno Guimaraes at the end for his service to the club, I will.

#2023. ‘We all fell in love with him’ – Hull coach shares what Lewis Koumas was like behind the scenes

A member of the coaching staff at Hull City has spoken very highly of what Lewis Koumas was like behind the scenes during his loan move at the MKM Stadium.

The Liverpool striker spent the second half of last season with the Tigers, playing a part in their promotion to the Premier League with three goals in 18 Championship appearances (including the play-offs).

He’s since become a fixed first-team player at Anfield, being handed five starts among his 14 appearances across all competitions and scoring in the Champions League victory over LASK in October.

Hull assistant coach Dean Holden spoke to The Redmen TV about how Koumas immediately won people over with his humility and hardworking attitude.

The 47-year-old said: “Within a week, everyone fell in love with him, from Stan on the door, the security guy, to the kitchen staff, kit men, the lot. We all fell in love with him.

“You know why? Just because he’s a real humble lad who just wants to be the best he can be and affects people around him in an energetic manner and just loves football.”

Holden went on to share anecdotes of Koumas being out on the training pitch along with Joe Gelhardt ’20 minutes out before everyone else is in the gym’, telling coaches not to ‘sugarcoat’ advice to him, and waiting patiently for his mother to collect him after he scored a late winner for Hull on his debut against Blackburn instead of ‘going out on the town and celebrating’.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

While we’re sure that the Liverpool youngster has been helped by sage advice from his father Jason, who graced the Premier League with West Brom and Wigan, the onus is still on him to put all of that bequeathed wisdom into action, and he’s most certainly doing that.

Andoni Iraola clearly has plenty of faith in the 21-year-old if he’s playing him regularly, even starting him against Manchester City (albeit that Alexander Isak wasn’t fit), and the young striker is repaying that trust with his performances on the pitch.

John Aldridge voiced his belief that the Wales international will ‘play for Liverpool for a long time‘, with Koumas standing out for his indefatigable pressing in the final third, which carries echoes of the beloved Bobby Firmino.

The stories shared by Holden testify to the tremendous attitude of the Reds youngster, who’s remained grounded and earned his place in the first-team squad to the extent that he’s nudged Federico Chiesa further down the pecking order.

We’re sure there’s still so much more to come from the Welshman, provided he can maintain the traits which have taken him this far already and (fingers crossed) avoid any major injury issues.

#2022. Lewis Hall desperate to leave Newcastle United and join Manchester United relegation scrap…really?

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Lewis Hall is the best English left-back by a country mile, Lewis Hall is the best left-back in the Premier League, Lewis Hall is going to join Manchester United in January 2027.

As we were reminded in this past week of internationals, Lewis Hall is indeed the Premier League’s and England’s best left-back.

The lifelong Newcastle United fan was the best player on the pitch when England defeated Croatia at Wembley on Thursday.

Then on Sunday he was up there as once again one of England’s very best players as they won 3-2 against World Cup holders Spain, with Lewis Hall outclassing their most dangerous player, Lamine Yamal.

So of course the natural outcome is that Lewis Hall will now sign for Manchester United in January…

Twenty years ago, Manchester United had won eight Premier League titles in the previous 14 seasons and never finished lower than third across that time period.

Back in November 2006, Manchester United were well on their way to reclaiming the Premier League title, they would win three in a row and five in seven, finishing runners-up in the other two.

From the 1991-92 season to the 2012-13 season, those 22 seasons saw Manchester United win 13 titles, six times runners-up, three times finishing third.

These last 13 seasons Manchester United have not won a single Premier League title, eight of the 13 they have finished outside the top three.

The last three Premier League seasons Manchester United have included a 15th place and an 8th place one and are currently sitting in the relegation zone after only one Premier League win in the last six months.

So of course Lewis Hall is desperate to join Manchester United…

The lifelong Newcastle United fan was eight years old when Man U last lifted the Premier League title.

Exactly why thirteen and a half years later would the best left-back in the Premier League would have even minimal interest  in signing for Manchester United?

Yet this is what the Manchester United fans, the Manchester United loving media, as well as other desperate idiots, want us all to believe.

Funnily enough, none of them give any reasons as to why this should be the case.

Nothing logical anyway, nothing that makes sense.

The best they would come out with is something along the lines of…”Well, it is Manchester United.”

Which ironically hits the nail squarely on the head, it is Manchester United.

It isn’t one of the successful clubs, it is one that used to be successful many years ago, during the first eight years Lewis Hall was on this earth, not the near decade and a half that has followed.

Lewis Hall now has the world at his feet and will have choices to make.

Will he stay forever at the club he and his family have supported all of their lives, or will he at some point join a club that appears to have a lot more chance of winning trophies?

Neither of those options feature Manchester United.

Yet I have seen so many journalists and pundits yet again embarrass themselves, after his stellar performances for England, talk about Lewis Hall set to move to Manchester United. Rather than talk about just how good he is for Newcastle United and vital to this current season (and hopefully beyond).

As an extra amusing aside, we also have the following…

On 29 May 2023 it was announced that Mauricio Pochettino would be appointed as head coach of Chelsea on 1 July 2023, on a two-year contract with an option to extend for another year.

On 22 August 2023, Lewis Hall joined Newcastle United on a season-long loan with an obligation to buy for £28 million, plus £7 million in add-ons (On 1 November, he scored his first goal for Newcastle United in a 3-0 League Cup win against Manchester United at Old Trafford. Then on 15 May 2024, Lewis Hall scored his first ever Premier League goal for United against Man U at Old Trafford…).

Amusingly, the new Manchester United boss Mauricio Pochettino was the Chelsea boss who sold Lewis Hall to Newcastle United. Pochettino selling Hall without even first playing him in a competitive match.

Of course, the reality is that at basket cases clubs Chelsea and Manchester United, the manager/head coach has no say in which players are bought or sold. So Mauricio Pochettino had no say on whether Chelsea sold Lewis Hall back in August 2023, just the same as Mauricio Pochettino will have no say in January 2027 if Manchester United embarrass themselves with an approach to try and ‘tempt’ (and fail, obviously) Lewis Hall to join Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Old Trafford circus.

Sean Steur was called up in the September international break for the Netherlands Under 21s, a very first time, thanks to the impressive early season Newcastle United form.

The 18-year-old then made his first ever appearance at that level for his country as the Netherlands played out a goalless draw at home to Norway on Friday 2 October, the teenager coming off the bench in the 83rd minute. Another call up in November and this time a two-legged European Championship qualifying play-off against the Denmark Under 21s.

In the first leg on Friday, the 18-year-old played very well as he helped the young Dutch side to a commanding 3-0 win, playing the opening 78 minutes and as well as an outstanding all action display, also provided an assist for the third goal.

The Netherlands U21s had one foot in next summer’s Under 21 European Championships finals after that 3-0 win in Denmark.

The return leg on Tuesday looking pretty much a formality but the young Danes had them sweating.

By the 52nd minute it was 3-1 to Denmark on the night and the Dutch only leading 4-3 on aggregate. However, a 71st minute goal dispelled any nerves and whilst the Netherlands lost 3-2 at home, it was a comfortable 5-3 victory on aggregate.

Sean Steur having another very good game and played the full match as he helped guide the Netherlands Under 21s into next summer’s Euros.

The value of international friendlies has always seemed questionable mid season: During a challenging domestic schedule the disruption of thousands of miles of travel, different coaching regimes and playing styles can easily prove disruptive: Let alone the risk of injuries to jaded players.

West Ham United have their fair share of absentees on international duty right now, which Scott Parker must be rueing as he tries to rebuild the playing style of the squad he has inherited from his predecessor.

However there’s an upside to  those international fixtures if it allows squad members to improve their game and their confidence – and several of the Hammers’ squad will come back to their club in far better spirits than they left.

As we covered yesterday Mads Hermansen’s headline winning performance to keep out Portugal can only have done him good.

International debut for Hammers youngster Mohamadou Kanté

Mohamadou Kanté must be made up at making his international debut for Mali – on the winning side in his first time wearing the national shirt means the midfield man will come back with a little more of a swagger than he left with, whilst news of Joel Piroe’s brace on international duty for Suriname will have been similarly well received at Rush Green.

With Castellanos and Pablo misfiring so badly, much is expected of the on-loan Leeds man and for Piroe to grab two goals in his national side’s 4-0 victory over Eswatini (formerly Swaziland, for anyone else who wondered) can only be a confidence boost for West Ham’s number nine ahead of the resumption of the Championship at the weekend.

#2016. West Ham Fans Asked to Unite in Memory of 19-Year-Old Supporter Luke

The loss of a young person reverberates far beyond their immediate family. Today, we are sharing Luke’s story in the hope of raising awareness, encouraging compassion, and supporting a tribute that means so much to those left behind.

Remembering Luke: A Young Life Gone Too Soon

At just 19 years old, Luke’s life was tragically cut short, leaving a family, circle of friends, and wider community struggling to come to terms with an unimaginable loss.

Known affectionately as “Lukey” and “Little Man” by those closest to him, Luke was a devoted West Ham United supporter and a loyal season ticket holder.

As they continue to navigate their grief, Luke’s family have made a simple but heartfelt request.

They are asking West Ham supporters attending the upcoming home fixture against Preston to join together in a minute of applause during the 19th minute of the match, marking the age at which Luke passed away.

The tribute is intended as a celebration of his life and a visible reminder that no family should feel alone during their darkest moments.

A shirt bearing Luke’s name will be placed on his seat in the stadium, providing a poignant symbol of the empty space left by his passing.

By sharing Luke’s story, we hope not only to support his family but also to encourage conversations around loss, grief, and the importance of supporting one another through difficult times.

C&H encourage anyone attending the match, or anyone who sees Luke’s story online, to help spread the word and support the planned tribute.

On the 19th minute, every clap will be a reminder that Luke’s life touched many people and that his memory continues to live on through his family, friends, and fellow supporters.

Our thoughts are with everyone who knew and loved Luke.

If this story resonates with you, please share it to help ensure Luke receives the tribute his family and friends are hoping for. Sometimes the smallest act of support can make the biggest difference.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

#2015. Cody Gakpo sticks up for much-maligned Liverpool teammate with ‘incredible football intelligence’

Cody Gakpo has heaped praise on one of his Liverpool teammates who boasts ‘incredible football intelligence’ and is an ‘extraordinary player’.

The 27-year-old will come up against fellow Reds star Florian Wirtz tonight when Netherlands face Germany in the UEFA Nations League. The Dutchman is also set for a reunion with his former Anfield boss Jurgen Klopp, who takes charge of the home side in Berlin.

LFC’s number 7 has faced some stinging criticism among the British media since his £100m move from Bayer Leverkusen in June 2025, but he went into the international window off the back of scoring one goal and setting up another in the 3-1 win at Crystal Palace eight days ago.

Speaking to the media ahead of tonight’s match, Gakpo was keen to highlight the standout traits of his Liverpool teammate.

The Dutch forward said of Wirtz (via GOAL): “Regarding his situation at the club, I think in his last match he played amazingly. He scored a goal, provided an assist, and was very important for us.

“As a team, we know the quality he possesses; he shows it in every match and training session. He is an extraordinary player.

“Coming to Liverpool with an expensive transfer fee certainly makes the adaptation process in this league not easy for anyone, even for players who have had a 10-year career here.

“However, he has incredible football intelligence. The way he reads and dictates the pace of the game is very important to our style of play. We are very happy to have him.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

With nine goals and 15 assists in 64 games for the Reds so far, it’d be fair to expect a higher return from Wirtz considering his position on the pitch and the transfer fee that the club paid for him.

However, the German is scintillating to watch when he’s at his best, and the win over Palace showed that he’s capable of bending matches to his will when he’s on song.

There have been other standout displays in recent weeks, including the game at Brentford when he created nine chances, and a terrific outing against Villarreal that he marked with a well-taken goal.

There are signs that Wirtz is now properly hitting his stride at Liverpool and primed to consistently turn in impactful performances, something he didn’t do often enough in his first season at Anfield.

Gakpo sees the 23-year-old at close quarters on a daily basis and is perfectly placed to speak about the German’s main qualities. On current form, our number 7 will be pivotal to our chances of success in the 2026/27 campaign.

#2014. West Ham player’s incredible injury statistic shows why he was the bargain of the summer

How managers and fitness conditioning teams must dread these international breaks – a player coming back with a serious injury picked up on duty for the national side must be every coaches’ fear. it seems a case of ‘so far so good’ for West Ham’s “international brigade” with no reports filtering through to Hammers HQ of new issues.

That does however leave the pre-existing condition: Manor Solomon’s frank admission to his national press will hardly reassure anyone at Rush Green. The winger has been struggling with a back injury and, according to sportwitness, this is neither a new issue nor one aggravated through too many games in the last window – which saw players asked to compete four times in twelve days for their nations:

“My back is something I’ve been dealing with for many years, ever since I was a teenager. I felt it during Saturday’s game; when I joined the national team, I felt fine, but by Tuesday, it had got worse, and I couldn’t train,” he said.

“Everyone knows how important the national team is to me and how hard it is for me to watch the team play while I’m not on the field. I hope I’ll be able to play on Tuesday.”

Facing a late fitness test, it seems Solomon is putting caution to one side in his desperation to be part of the Israel national team to take on Austria tomorrow.

Sadly, there is nothing new here, the old ‘club v country‘ debate in which domestic football (paying the players’ massive wages) gets a lesser priority from a player who will stop at nothing and go through the pain to play for his country.

Solomon looked like the deal of the decade after his first couple of outings, having joined West Ham for a mere £5 million up front.

More disclosures about his back issues and many and varied other problems – which have led him to sit out an incredible 860 days since the start of his career in 2018 ( according to sportwitness) make the price look more understandable by the week.

West Ham will have to cope with a player who has huge fitness issues but who doesn’t apparently, want to listen to his body, rather playing through the pain to represent his country. It’s not a combination that is likely preserve his longevity in the sport.

#2012. Man United hope Marcus Rashford will be back for huge Liverpool clash after fresh treatment plan on groin injury given by specialist

Published: 12:00 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 12:00 EST, 11 November 2026

Manchester United hope Marcus Rashford can be fit for their next game at Liverpool a week on Sunday after the England star began a new treatment programme.

Rashford returned to Old Trafford in the summer after a year on loan at Barcelona having sustained a hip injury at the World Cup.

The 29-year-old played in the first six league games of the season – as well as the Carabao Cup tie against Brighton and, most recently, the Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid in mid-October – but aggravated the problem which has spread to his groin.

Rashford visited a groin specialist in Dublin last week with a member of United’s medical staff and a new recovery programme has now been put in place.

Rashford is said to have a good relationship with Michael Carrick and wanted to give the head coach his support.

But playing while carrying the injury only made it worse. It’s understood that he even offered to go on the bench at Chelsea recently but the club decided against it.

Man United star Marcus Rashford is seen in a TikTok posted by his hairdresser on Tuesday

Rashford is hoping to be back and available for the game against Liverpool

However, Rashford will continue to work his way back to fitness during the international break and United hope he will be available for the trip to Anfield to face Liverpool.

With Carrick expected to be sacked and replaced by Mauricio Pochettino, it could well be the Argentine’s first game in charge on his return to the Premier League having previously managed Tottenham, Chelsea and Southampton.

Rashford has an impressive record against Liverpool with seven goals in 20 appearances against United’s biggest rivals.

#2011. Champions League draw: Arsenal to renew Mourinho rivalry with Real Madrid tie

Arsenal will host old nemesis José Mourinho’s Real Madrid in the league phase of the Champions League.

Mourinho, the former Chelsea, Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur manager, will return to London to resume hostilities against last season’s beaten finalists.

Other reunions from Thursday’s draw include Manchester City travelling to Barcelona, to whom they last week sold Rodri, and Liverpool visiting Inter Milan, who have signed Curtis Jones.

Arsenal will also travel to Harry Kane’s Bayern Munich, while United will host the Germans as well on their Champions League return in a repeat of the legendary 1999 final. Michael Carrick’s side will also visit Cesc Fàbregas’s Como.

Mourinho last managed at the Emirates Stadium in March 2021, barely a month before his sacking by Spurs.

During his two spells as Chelsea manager, Mourinho famously had run-ins with Arsenal’s Arsène Wenger.

Mourinho called Wenger a “specialist in failure” after the Frenchman failed to add to his three Premier League titles following his Portuguese counterpart’s arrival in London in 2004.

Last season, Mikel Arteta finally ended Arsenal’s long wait to be crowned champions of England but agonisingly missed out on European glory.

Verdict Premier League champions should not be daunted by any game, but Real Madrid – with Mourinho in control – has the feel of a defining match of the group stage. Facing Kane in Munich does not seem any easier. Some tough assignments here including a trip to Napoli but the pot-four teams seem straightforward for Mikel Arteta.

Verdict Playing against the European champions and travelling to Barcelona will be a true test of how much progress Enzo Maresca has made in the short time he has been at the Etihad Stadium. City’s other games do not look easy either but they should be defeating teams such as Sporting Lisbon and Porto – at least they would be expected to under Pep Guardiola.

Verdict The San Siro was where Arne Slot began to turn results around last season and Iraola getting a win there would be a big statement. Atlético staged a comeback at Anfield in 2020 and the repeat fixture will be tight. But there are enough winnable games there for Liverpool to reach the next round.

Verdict They will face a wall of noise in Istanbul when they play Galatasaray, but Villa will look to get points from the game. There are some tasty destinations for travelling fans and getting results there will ease the pressure on the match against PSG, who have been rattled by Villa before but remain a difficult opponent. The Nou Camp is a place where momentum can change in a season – for good or bad.

Verdict The repeat of the 1999 final is the standout fixture, but Michael Carrick should be looking beyond that match for the points needed to progress. He has been given a tough set of away games to navigate. They are winnable but difficult. So those games at Old Trafford will be very important.

That brings our coverage of the Champions League draw to an end, as the 36 teams found which eight teams they will be facing in the league phase of this season’s tournament. Thanks for joining us!

The league phase will kick off on 8 September and will be wrapped up after all teams play at the same time on 27 January.

The top eight teams of the league phase progress to the last 16 automatically, while teams that finish between ninth and 24th will be forced to navigate a play-off tie to reach the knockout stages.

So we have 144 fixtures decided but there are certainly a few heavyweight contests which stand out:

That brings the draw to an end! Just a reminder that the order of the fixtures is based on the pots and the respective home and away fixtures within the pots, rather than chronology.

That is pots two and three done. Just the pot four teams to sort out now, finding out which other pot four teams they will face.

Some crackers in there. Up next we will be finding out all the opponents for the pot two teams.

The draw is now getting underway. Uefa deputy general secretary Giorgio Marchetti comes on stage to oversee proceedings. A reminder of the format:

The 36 teams will be split into four pots of nine, based on “club coefficient rankings”, with defending champions Paris St-Germain automatically named as the top seed.

Proceedings will begin with a team from pot one being drawn at random, and they will be allocated eight fixtures – four at home and four away – by an automated software. They will face two teams from each pot, with one home game and one away game per pot, while they cannot play a team from their country.

This will be done for all nine teams from pot one, before the same process takes place for pot two teams, though they will already know their pot one opponents. Pot three teams will then find out their pot three and four opponents, before the pot four sides are allocated their fixtures against each other.

But before the draw we will be hearing from Villa about the 2011 final, which he scored in as Barcelona dismantled Manchester United at Wembley.

He calls it a “great generation” of players, mentioning Lionel Messi, who also scored in the 3-1 win.

Henry will be part of the draw so he remains on stage as Ceferin departs. David Villa will also be coming onto the stage to help with proceedings. We are told the draw will be starting shortly.

We’re hearing from Henry now about losing the 2006 Champions League final with Arsenal and winning three years later with Barcelona.

He’s now discussing the current Arsenal crop and how they are getting closer to the trophy. He says if “they keep their core” and make some additions they can get over the line. But PSG “are an annoying team at the moment”.

Marquinhos on winning the respect award: “I’m very happy and honoured to be given this trophy. Fair play is an essential part of both football and daily life, and I will keep being respectful this year.”

Up next is the “Uefa President’s Award”? The winner is of course Thierry Henry and, fortunately, he is in attendance, so he’s up on the stage to collect this honour. A slow clap from Martin Keown in the crowd.

Reshmin Chowdhury and Pedro Pinto shuffle the musicians off the stage before outlining this evening’s itinerary.

Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin is then brought up to the stage, after a quiet summer, to announce Marquinhos as the winner of a new award, the Respect Beyond the Game award.

Marquinhos is not at the ceremony, so it will be PSG president Nasser Al-Khelaifi coming up to collect it. We hear from the defender on a video message.

The ceremony is underway in Monaco with a live performance of the famous anthem – orchestra and all – while pictures of previous winners play on the big screen in the background.

Proceedings will begin with a team from pot one being drawn at random, and they will be allocated eight fixtures – four at home and four away – by an automated software. They will face two teams from each pot, with one home game and one away game per pot, while they cannot play a team from their country.

This will be done for all nine teams from pot one, before the same process takes place for pot two teams, though they will already know their pot one opponents. Pot three teams will then find out their pot three and four opponents, before the pot four sides are allocated their fixtures against each other.

There are five English teams involved in the Champions League this season – one short of the Premier League’s tally from last term.

All set for this evening's #UCL draw in Monaco 📌🏆 pic.twitter.com/N3verDUO9y

Paris St-Germain will be aiming to become the first team to win three successive Champions Leagues since Real Madrid’s run of titles between 2016 and 2018.

The holders 🔴🔵#UCLdraw pic.twitter.com/eB05BNfWZi

This season is the third under the new format, with a league phase instead of a group stage, and Uefa has confirmed that fixtures that have taken place in the league phase of the two previous seasons cannot be repeated this time around.

For example, Liverpool cannot host Real Madrid in the league phase this term after welcoming the 15-time European champions to Anfield at this stage of the previous two campaigns. Andoni Iraola’s side could, however, travel to the Bernabeu for an away meeting with Madrid.

Similarly, Arsenal will not be travelling to San Siro to face Inter, but could host the Serie A champions at the Emirates.

Arsenal finished top of the league phase last season after winning all eight fixtures and it resulted in a favourable run to the final, facing Bayer Leverkusen, Sporting and Atletico Madrid.

Liverpool, meanwhile, topped the league phase in the 2024-25 campaign – the first season with the new format – but fell at the first hurdle in the knockout stages after being drawn against Paris St-Germain.

The Ligue 1 side have proven that it’s not essential to be firing the whole way through the tournament, finishing 15th and 11th in the league phase in the last two seasons but going on to lift the trophy on both occasions.

Liverpool, Manchester City and Arsenal will be among the teams joining the Parisians in pot one, while the two remaining English teams, Manchester United and Aston Villa, will be in pot two.

Proceedings will begin with a team from pot one being drawn at random, and they will be allocated eight fixtures – four at home and four away – by an automated software. They will face two teams from each pot, with one home game and one away game per pot, while they cannot play a team from their country.

This will be done for all nine teams from pot one, before the same process takes place for pot two teams, though they will already know their pot one opponents. Pot three teams will then find out their pot three and four opponents, before the pot four sides are allocated their fixtures against each other.

This season is the third under the new format, with a league phase instead of a group stage, and Uefa has confirmed that fixtures that have taken place in the league phase of the two previous seasons cannot be repeated this time around.

For example, Liverpool cannot host Real Madrid in the league phase this term after welcoming the 15-time European champions to Anfield at this stage of the previous two campaigns. Andoni Iraola’s side could, however, travel to the Bernabeu for an away meeting with Madrid.

The league phase will kick off on 8 September and will be wrapped up after all teams play at the same time on 27 January. The top eight teams of the league phase progress to the last 16 automatically, while teams that finish between ninth and 24th will be forced to navigate a play-off tie to reach the knockout stages.

The draw is expected to get underway at 5pm.
