#1956. Hassocks downed by Dockers for second time this season

Three times Hassocks have lost in the Southern Combination Premier Division so far this season. Two of those defeats have come at the hands of Newhaven.

The 2-1 scoreline at the Trafalgar Ground was the same as when the Dockers sailed back from Mid Sussex with all three points in August. The Robins must be delighted to see the back of Newhaven in the league.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

So often the scourge of Hassocks in the past, Lee Robinson scored both the Dockers goals in the space of seven second half minutes.

Lewis Finney pulled one back with 13 minutes remaining and although the Robins threw the kitchen sink at Newhaven, they were unable to find another way through.

The Dockers defence were outstanding and in particular ex-Hassocks centre back Matt Gunn, who deservedly picked up the host's man-of-the-match award afterwards.

Gunn was also a threat at the other end and had two chances to score twice himself inside the opening three minutes. He first saw a flicked header from a corner sensationally tipped around the post by Ed Cooper.

That resulted in another corner and although the Robins cleared this one, Newhaven were able to recycle possession and get a delivery from Ezra Roeg into the box. Gunn remained forward and met it with a powerful headed effort just over the bar.

Hassocks were unable to cope with the relentless tempo at which the Dockers had started. A situation summed up when Harry Reed and Tom Sekyere converged rapidly on Jack Troak to snare the ball from him.

The intense press got Tyler Capon in down the right flank for a cross which Cooper and Harvey Blake combined to clear in somewhat unorthodox, acrobatic style to prevent Robinson from having a tap-in.

Troak managed to lead an attack which finally broke the Robins out of their own half. His cross hung up into the middle was met by Dan Perry for a header just over.

Perry was making his Hassocks debut after signing from East Grinstead Town in midweek. The Hitman has netted 11 times this season for the Wasps and looks to be a quality addition.

Dan Turner then saw a shot from the edge of the box blocked by the nether regions of Elliott Bresciani. The defender putting his body on the line was an early sign of the sort of defending Newhaven would deploy to good effect to get them over the line in the second half.

With the Robins now a willing participant in the game, things began to ebb and flow from end-to-end. Capon was millimetres away from connecting with a Reed centre and Cooper did just enough to put off Sekyere into placing a one-on-one wide.

Perry looked the most likely source of goals for Hassocks. He drew a routine save from Jake Rhodes when heading a Harvey Blake cross on target.

Rhodes then pulled off a much more difficult reaction stop at close range when Big Alex Fair delivered and Perry stooped to direct a header across the Dockers goalkeeper.

Cooper saved well at his near post when Matt Feeney-Hill cut inside before Newhaven faded a little in the final 10 minutes of the half, probably because of the speed at which they played the previous 35.

As a result, Hassocks were on top in the period leading into the break. Finney saw a shot blocked by Gunn and some nifty footwork from Fair followed by a clever back heel teed up Omar Abdsami for a shot just a little too high.

The second half was a slow-burner in comparison to the first until Robinson fired the Dockers ahead on 63 minutes. Sekyere hooked a hopeful ball over the top of the Hassocks defence which the veteran forward showed a remarkable turn of pace to latch onto.

It carried Robinson clear of Turner and enabled him to curl a fine finish with his side foot around Cooper and into the far corner.

Newhaven doubled their lead with 70 on the clock after the Robins were unconvincing dealing with a corner. The delivery from Feeney-Hill was only half cleared to the edge of the box, allowing Ross Barclay to return an up-and-under into the area.

Gunn won a flick on and it found the unmarked Robinson, who had taken advantage of a slapdash Hassocks offside line to move front and centre of goal where he volleyed home unmarked.

Half-hearted appeals for the goal to be disallowed were easily dismissed. Robinson had stayed in a legal position, thanks in part to the Robins being completely out of shape.

Hassocks now had no choice but to lay siege on the Newhaven goal. Liam Benson came on as James Westlake changed formation and went with two up front.

The adjustment helped the Robins. Tall striker Jamie Wilkes put an awkward header wide and Devon Fender rattled the post with a good volley from inside the D.

An excellent move halved the deficit on 77 minutes. Abdsami was patient in waiting for a gap to appear into which he could play a forward pass.

When it came, his ball into the feet of Benson was superbly flicked around the corner by the substitute and into the path of Finney.

The finish from Finney was cool as you like as he picked out the far corner with aplomb to move onto double figures for the season.

Hassocks now had 13 minutes in which to try and find an equaliser. Unfortunately, their shooting from that point on did not match the calmness or precision with which Finney had pulled one back.

Finney came closest to providing a leveller on 88. Abdsami crossed and Perry directed a clever downwards header into the penalty box. The arriving Finney met it with a rasping volley which Rhodes somehow flung himself upwards to block.

Bresciani produced an overhead kick to clear the loose ball off the line and prevent Benson putting away the rebound. In a moment which summed the afternoon up really for Hassocks, that clearance gave another chance to Blake.

The Robins captain could only blaze so high as to pose more of a threat to Newhaven Fort all the way up the hill than the Dockers goal.

Other than the quality of the Finney finish, there was one other positive for the Robins to take home at least. Raging Joe Bull made his 300th senior appearance for the club, becoming the first Robin to pass the triple century landmark since Phil Gault a decade ago.

Hassocks: Cooper; Blake, D Turner, Hendy, Bull; Wilkes, Finney; Fair, Abdsami, Troak; Perry.

Subs: Fender, Benson, Budd (used), Croal, Brodie (unused).

#1955. Rangers pay tribute following death of club great Ralph Brand

Rangers have paid tribute to club great Ralph Brand, who has died at the age of 89.

One of the most prolific strikers in the club's history, Brand contributed 222 goals in 347 appearances for Rangers over an 11-year spell at Ibrox between 1954 and 1965. He later played for Manchester City, Sunderland, Raith Rovers and Hamilton Academical.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Brand won 11 major honours during his time with the Light Blues and played in the Treble winning side of 1963-64. As well as lifting four Scottish titles, he also won four League Cup and three Scottish Cup winner's medals, the latter set achieved in consecutive years in which he was a scorer in every final, the only player to have achieved that feat.

He won eight Scotland caps and scored eight goals - no mean feat during a time when Denis Law was also in his prime.

Born and raised in Edinburgh, Brand was signed for Rangers by the late, great Bill Struth in 1952 after he impressed for Scotland Schoolboys in a match against their English counterparts at Wembley. He formed a famed strike partnership with fellow Edinburgh native Jimmy Millar in what was considered a golden period for the club.

“When Bill Struth signed me, Rangers were the club to play for,” Brand once remarked. “There were a number of clubs in for me from south of the border – big clubs too – but the only team I ever wanted to play for was Glasgow Rangers, and that’s a fact.”

Brand was also part of the Rangers side that reached the Cup Winners Cup final in 1961, becoming the first British team to contest a European final, before losing 4-1 to Fiorentina over two legs, home and away.

The club announced his passing in a statement which read: "The Rangers family is today mourning the loss of Hall of Fame forward, Ralph Brand, at the age of 89.

"A penalty box forward who would scarcely look out of place in the modern game, Brand’s strike partnership with Jimmy Millar stands alone in Rangers folklore. In many ways, it is impossible to think about one without thinking about the other; a double act which supercharged a glorious era for Gers supporters in the late 1950s and early 1960s. Where Millar was the steel; Brand was the silk.

"Ralph Brand’s contribution to Rangers was vast and, through his Hall of Fame recognition, he will forever be remembered as a great of the club. The thoughts of everyone at Rangers are with his loved ones at this sad time."

#1954. ‘Predictable, mutual, unfair’ - A brief history of Brighton’s sacked managers

So the current worst kept secret in football is out. Michael Carrick is no more at Old Trafford, it’s actually not United’s first rodeo in this footballing genre.

I recall being at the Amex on Easter Monday 2014, in the period of about 15 minutes I and four others in our party of ten that day received a forwarded text stating that David Moyes would be sacked as Manchester United manager the following morning, Tuesday 22nd April, and he was!

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Sackings are, unfortunately part and parcel of football. In my time following the Albion, we’ve had dismissals that have been predictable, justified, unfair and even a tad bizarre.

My first was Pat Saward in October 1973. I didn’t know much about, but in researching my book a couple of years ago, it was clear that once the ultra ambitious Albion chairman Mike Bamber got a sniff he might be able to rock the football world and bring Brian Clough to the Goldstone, dear old Pat was a dead man walking.

We then didn’t get another sacking for nearly a decade, and then it was all decided on the doorsteps of Sussex.

Mike Bailey had got the club it’s highest ever league finish, 13th in 81/82. But he was building from the back and at times the football wasn’t that exciting. Crowds dipped below the all important break even 15,000, and when fans were questioned by the lottery sellers on their weekly rounds, the word ‘boring’ was predominant and Bailey was out.

All these years later, I still believe the decision was a tad unfair and short sighted, but also one of those classic Brighton and Hove Albion sliding door moments.

Albion legend Steve Foster recently told me, whilst we probably wouldn’t have got to the 1983 Cup Final, we wouldn’t have got relegated and in time, Bailey could have turned us into a consistently top ten side, regularly challenging for Europe.

Bailey’s successor, Jimmy Melia, was almost in a footballing Sword of Damocles situation. Initially a caretaker boss, within a month the Albion embarked on an FA Cup campaign. With Bamber effectively waiting to wield the axe the Monday after the Albion were knocked out, but they weren’t. Melia, with his white dancing shoes took the Albion to Wembley but also rock bottom of the First Division and relegation!

Chris Cattlin was the next cab on the rank, his near three year tender, on a limited budget saw the Albion compete and again, like Bailey, given time, and funding, who knows what he could have achieved?

But he was unceremoniously dismissed at the end of the 85/86 season, but took the Albion to court for unfair dismissal, which resulted in his final victory at the club.

The returning Alan Mullery, another Goldstone legend, in the summer of 1986, was purely cosmetic. Replacing the popular Cattlin with the equally popular Mullery, saw a spike in season ticket sales, and not a lot more.

Mullery was a patsy, disgracefully treated when sacked in January 1987 for almost laughable reasons with the Albion in 13th.

A wretched run under new boss Barry Lloyd followed, with, as with the Division One exit in 1983, the Albion were relegated to the old Third Division in 22nd place in the division.

Yet we had to wait another nine years for another dismissal. Lloyd had left by mutual consent in December 1993, but in December 1996, with the cash strapped and soon to be homeless Albion in 92nd place in the Football League, Jimmy Case was unsurprisingly axed.

As was his successor, Steve Gritt, despite working a footballing miracle and keeping Albion in the league, he was gone in early 1998, again unjust, more about finance than football.

Exiled at Gillingham, crowds nowhere near break even, a massive shot in the arm was required, and that came in the shape of another returning legend (pattern forming) Brian Horton.

Jeff Wood, a genuinely nice guy, was in the wrong place at the wrong time Albion wise in 1999, as was Martin Hinshelwood in 2002.

Full disclosure, I’m in the privileged position to call a number of ex Albion bosses friends, and Mark McGhee is firmly in that catergory. His dismissal in September 2006, is another that sticks in the craw.

I do however still have a degree of sympathy in the bigger picture. At the time, Dick Knight, chasing our collective Falmer dream, was juggling all the balls whilst protecting his own.

Dean Wilkins, still in my opinion technically one of the best coaches the club has ever had, was both a safe pair of hands but a far cheaper option whilst the battle for the stadium went on, tellingly though however he has never worked as a manager since he departed the club in 2008.

I still believe that Mark McGhee would have mounted a promotion challenge to get us back in the Championship.

With the greatest respect in my opinion Albion wise Russel Slade still remains an irrelevance, only doing the job that Micky Adams would have done had he not resigned in February 2009.

Which brings us on to Gus Poyet, a footballing firework, it was great whilst it lasted, but it was what it was, and given off field working relationships, or lack of them, it was never going to last.

But to clarify Gus was not sacked live in the BBC, he was fully aware of the situation and his subsequent reaction was as genuine as American Wrestling!

But he still gave us some great memories, which will never be forgotten.

Chris Hughton’s sacking in 2019, was another exit, which leaves a bad taste. It could have been handled so much better. Like the Moyes text of 2014, I was told that Graham Potter was coming in 40 minutes before Hughton kicked off what was to be his final Albion game. Yet he was interviewed by Richie Reynolds on the pitch at the end about his hopes for the next season!

Potter, could and should have been sacked at least one or two occasions, but a crumb of comfort was the £20 million Chelsea gave us for his services, it truly is a funny old game.

So was Roberto De Zerbi sacked in May 2024, or merely his contract not renewed?

I still love his time as Albion manager, like Gus and others some amazing memories, but unfortunately there are boundaries and as soon as that microphone went under his nose in Rome with the apparent diatribe against Tony Bloom there was only going to be one outcome.

Which brings us around to Fab. Yes many, myself included, have embarked on the ‘Hurzeler Hokey Cokey’, but given the Albion’s current fortunes that’s well and truly parked.

You can never say never following the Albion but I think it’s a fairly safe bet there won’t be another Amex sacking anytime soon!

#1953. Huddersfield Town chief Martin Drury highlights where Sean Roughan has transformed his Terriers' fortunes

While the on-pitch transformation in fortunes for the striker—one of the form players in League One so far this season—has been a standout feature of the Terriers' blossoming campaign, there have been other tales to savour for the league leaders.

Among them is the rise to prominence of defender Sean Roughan, who is starting to show the form which alerted Town to his potential during his yeoman service at Lincoln City.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The Irishman has impressed after casting aside an untimely thigh injury sustained in the club's opening game of the season in early August, the Carabao Cup tie against Preston North End.

Roughan, 23, has not looked back since being restored to the starting line-up for the game at Plymouth Argyle on October 17.

The Dubliner was excellent in the 2-0 victory at a high-flying competitor at the top end of the third tier, after stepping in for the injured Murray Wallace, and has started the club's last five league matches.

That spell, in which Town have been unbeaten, has seen Martin Drury's side pick up an eye-catching 13 points from a possible 15 ahead of Saturday's mouth-watering test against another form side in Leicester City, who visit the Accu Stadium.

Along the way, Roughan also laid a ghost to rest.

After a very tough appointment at Bradford City last autumn - when Town were humbled 3-1—he played an instrumental part in the visitors turning things around at Valley Parade this season in a 3-0 victory on Hallowe'en.

Head coach Drury, whose side are three-quarters of the way through a run of four successive home games in all competitions, said: "I've really been impressed by Sean's mentality this season.

"He's been out injured and he's missed some time. He's come back into the team. I think he's showing more leadership and he's more vocal and he's competing.

"It was a tough game at Bradford because they play long balls and diagonal balls and you're constantly fighting and scrapping and it's not a clean game. I felt his mentality was strong throughout that game and it has been in other games.

"So a lot of credit needs to go to Sean and the medical and performance staff for the way they brought him back."

#1952. Liverpool Confidential: Why Will Wright is the breakout star of Reds academy - LEWIS STEELE reveals club's plans for 6ft 3in hat-trick hero, his rise from Euxton Villa to Anfield and why coaches believe he's Andoni Iraola's next big thing

Published: 12:00 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 16:17 EST, 11 November 2026

On Will Wright’s last two trips abroad, he has needed to check in some extra baggage on the return flight.

Two UEFA Youth League away games, two hat-tricks and a pair of match balls to go with them. It’s now 13 goals for the season for 18-year-old Wright after his treble in a 5-3 win at Fenerbahce last week, and he has earned a first England youth call-up to boot.

Another hat-trick in one of those three games for the Young Lions? You wouldn’t bet against it – but Wright is used to these rapid rises.

Eighteen months ago, the 6ft 3in striker signed for Liverpool on a Friday, passed his driving test at 8am the next morning and then played for the first team the day after in a friendly at Anfield.

Now, the former Salford City striker is the name on everyone’s lips around Kirkby – with many thinking he could be the next cab off the rank from Liverpool’s famed academy.

Will Wright has lit up the academy goal charts this season for Liverpool, scoring a pair of hat-tricks in the UEFA Youth League

The Under 19s captain struck a brilliant treble against Fenerbahce last week to take his season tally to 13

Wright was first spotted by Salford scouts when playing for local side Euxton Villa, a ninth-tier club who have two England internationals among their alumni in David Unsworth and Sam Johnstone. Wright’s father, Mark, coached at Euxton and is an ex-professional for Preston North End.

It was an unusual path as most future stars are normally signed up by their mid-teens but Wright had injury issues amid a growth spurt that took him to the lanky frame that now bullies defenders. He had heel issues and has worked with a specialist on fascia problems.

Wright made his Salford debut in an 8-0 FA Cup defeat by Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City in January 2025 but scouts had already been alerted by his 50-goal haul at youth level. Arsenal, led by then-academy chief Per Mertesacker, launched an aggressive approach to sign him.

At one point, Liverpool signalled to Wright and Salford that they were pulling out of the deal, given Arsenal’s interest was so advanced. But the Reds soon returned to prevent the Gunners signing their next ‘Wrighty’.

The deal was worth peanuts in the grand scheme of things, around £300,000. It is good money for League Two Salford, though, and they will be set for additional payments for first-team appearances, honours and future national team caps.

Wright, who has a younger brother and is a Nike athlete, is a throwback No9. It is easy to reach for comparisons to current players but the way he combines pace, power and prolific finishing is not too dissimilar to Erling Haaland.

He is a strong dribbler and scored a fantastic solo goal for Liverpool's Under 21s against Rochdale in the EFL Trophy in September, receiving possession on the touchline around halfway, tricking his way past two defenders and curling a sumptuous effort into the top corner.

He is the captain of the Under 19s team and I have watched him play live several times, including one game last season where he was clearly targeted by Atletico Madrid defenders. The striker was clattered, suffered a medial ligament injury and was sidelined for several months.

He is a strong dribbler and scored a fantastic solo goal for Liverpool's Under 21s against Rochdale in the EFL Trophy in September

Coaches have pinpointed hold-up play and heading as two things to work on, as well as instructing Wright not to ‘rise to the bait’ of bigger defenders who might try to ruffle him up

He has returned with a vengeance, with a hat-trick against LASK last month and then last week's effort against Fenerbahce. What impressed more in the latter was not his goals – one a penalty, the other two both true poachers’ finishes – but his assist.

Wright was on a hat-trick at the time but, instead of shooting, he played a ball to Finn Inglethorpe – son of academy director Alex – to score. Earlier, Wright and Josh Sonni-Lambie had argued over who was to take a penalty. Wright won the row and scored.

Under 21s boss Rob Page told the pair later that he would rather them show hunger to score and passion rather than shy away. Page is a huge fan of Wright and said: ‘There was a real maturity about his performance. One of the parts of the development for all the forwards is being unselfish in their actions.

‘As much as he wants to see the headlines and be successful himself, it is all about sharing that. Will has done that really well today with a hat-trick, a complete performance.’

Pressed on how far away Wright is from the first team, Page replied: ‘He doesn’t have to worry about that. Just bring the best version of yourself every day in training, give absolutely everything in games as he does. The rest will take care of itself.

‘He’s got a great support around him. His family are very supportive. Alex (Inglethorpe) is there to lean on, he’s got myself and Jay (Spearing, academy coach). He never gets carried away.’

Coaches have pinpointed hold-up play and heading as two things to work on, as well as instructing Wright not to ‘rise to the bait’ of bigger defenders who might try to ruffle him up. They have also worked on his off-the-ball runs to the back post.

So, what next? It is understood a January loan is being considered. Liverpool think toughening up Wright in a senior league could be a step worth taking, having used him in each of the last two pre-seasons. His agent was at the AXA Training Centre on Tuesday and there will be no shortage of clubs willing to take him on.

Liverpool think toughening up Wright in a senior league could be a step worth taking, having used him in each of the last two pre-seasons

Wright got six minutes off the bench against Como in a friendly at Anfield in August, coming on for Alexander Isak up front

Andoni Iraola will be consulted, too. He has called up the likes of Trey Nyoni, Lewis Koumas and Luke Chambers this season and is eager to use young stars.

Iraola is in frequent dialogue with youth staff such as Page, Inglethorpe, plus Luiz Fernando Iubel who is often cited as the ‘link’ between the academy and first team.

The Brazilian has been spotted at several academy games this term, including for Wright’s hat-trick in Turkey where Iubel sat alongside sporting director Julian Ward and loans manager Gary Probert.

Whether a first-team breakthrough comes now or in the future, the future for Wright looks bright.

Dominik Szoboszlai’s participation with Hungary this week remains in the balance with the national team doing all they can to get their captain fit for crunch games.

The Hungarians take on Georgia and Northern Ireland in must-win Nations League matches – and may have to go without their star man. Szoboszlai hurt his knee in the win at Crystal Palace and, after an injury-hit six weeks, could do with a rest.

But he will try his best to be fit for national team duty and a decision will not be made until the 11th hour.

It comes after Virgil van Dijk pulled out of Dutch duty with a minor muscle issue. It is believed he has been managing the problem for at least a month and was surprised to be substituted on to the field against LASK — which might explain the team conceding three after he came on!

Virgil van Dijk (left) has pulled out of international duty and Dominik Szoboszlai (right) could be set to follow him

Confidential readers will recall our musings on Harvey Elliott a fortnight ago, with Valencia sources telling us that the La Liga outfit might consider cancelling his loan in January.

The English midfielder had struggled in Spain for fitness and form. He was then sent off against Villarreal but, as we reported, Valencia would give him another chance to prove his worth.

He has started well, scoring a free-kick in what was his first start for any club in 285 days. It was part of a notable 6-0 win in the Copa del Rey.

Elliott ran over to fans and put his arms aloft appearing to apologise, which adds to his comments a week ago about the red card where he said: ‘I made a mistake and I’m truly sorry. It won’t happen again.’

#1949. Man United transfer news: Mauricio Pochettino faces battle for 'impressive' £21m centre-back from Liverpool and Chelsea

Manchester United share interest in AC Milan defender Koni De Winter with Liverpool and Chelsea, the newest report has claimed.

The Red Devils are preparing for the return of Premier League football, with Mauricio Pochettino set to take charge of his first game on November 22 against Liverpool.

There are concerns that his weak defence could cost the new head coach at Anfield, with the likes of Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martinez having struggled this season.

Recruiting new defenders should be seen as a priority, and it should come as no surprise to see the club linked with a host of talented stars.

Pochettino is known to use an aggressive system, with the 54-year-old often asking defenders to step forward and press from the halfway line.

De Winter possesses immense speed, and the 24-year-old is far more mobile then any of United's current options at the back.

The Belgian has been trusted on the ball by Milan, with the centre-back so far averaging 61.1 successful passes per game in Serie A.

De Winter also wins most of his battles in the air, and he could be a sensible addition in either January or the summer.

Both Liverpool and Chelsea will almost certainly qualify for European competitions this season, whereas United are fighting a relegation battle.

However, the Reds may not need to sign a centre-back if Virgil van Dijk extends his stay beyond this summer, though the Blues are always active in the market.

Pochettino may find it hard to convince De Winter to join, especially if Chelsea secure either Champions League or Europa League football, and it remains to be seen if Old Trafford will still be the attraction it once was for transfer targets.

#1948. Jurgen Klopp loves him but Brajan Gruda may never play for Brighton again

Brajan Gruda arrived at Brighton in 2024 as one of Europe's hottest prospects.

Albion paid around £25m to Mainz for the German playmaker as he joined on a four-year contract.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

"I saw the big impact he made in the Bundesliga and he's a player I admire a lot," said Brighton’s German head coach Fabian Hurzeler at the time.

Hurzeler also admired Gruda's style of play and describe the then 20-year-old as a "street footballer."

Jurgen Klopp used the same "street baller" term this week as Gruda - now 22 - made an impressive start to his senior Germany career.

He netted a fine individual goal on his full debut against Serbia last week and then grabbed a goal and two assists as Germany walloped the Netherlands 5-0 last night. Brighton's Bart Verbruggen was in goal for the Dutch.

After Gruda's excellent debut against Serbia, Klopp said he felt sorry for their left back Petar Sukacev. "That left-back, he's a poor lad!" said the former Liverpool boss Klopp.

Opta statistics backed up Klopp’s claim as they stated nine of Gruda's 14 dribbles against Serbia were successful.

"He's a fantastic player who loves to take people on and hasn't yet fulfilled his potential. He doesn't need to at his age, but he's shown an awful lot of positive signs," Klopp said.

So will he play for Brighton again and why did the Seagulls loan him out? Gruda made 45 appearances for Albion under Hurzeler in all competitions and showed glimpses of his potential with four goals and eight assists.

Niggling injuries and the fitness demands of the Premier League saw Gruda struggle to make a sustained impact. At times he featured in the No 10 role but largely he was behind the powerful Yankuba Minteh for the right wing slot.

Minteh joined for £30m in the same window as Gruda but the Gambian adapted faster. Gruda made just eight Premier League starts in the 2025-26 season and a change of environment was deemed beneficial by all parties and he joined RB Leipzig on loan for the second half of last campaign

“Brajan wants regular football, and we are not able to guarantee him that in the second half of the season," said Hurzeler.

Three goals and three assists for Leipzig in the Bundesliga convinced them to extend the loan for another season and Brighton were happy to sanction another temporary deal.

Sporting director Mike Cave said, “Brajan had a good second half of the season with Leipzig and was keen to explore the opportunity of remaining there for the coming year.

“This is a move that allows Brajan to continue to secure regular playing time at a good level, in an environment he knows well.”

Brighton are pretty sharp on their loan agreements but no doubt they will now be double checking the small print of the loan contract.

Leipzig are believed to have an obligation to buy at the end of the season, albeit with certain conditions - but the size of any potential transfer fee remains unclear.

His value is clearly going upwards and the loan agreement will likely allow Brighton to cash in, should they decide to sell. Further high-profile displays for Klopp's Germany will see that increase.

Gruda remains contracted with Albion until 2028 and this week Bayern Munich and Bayer Leverkusen were also credited with interest.

Transfer expert Florian Plettenberg posted: “The obligation to buy for Brajan Gruda will be activated in 2027 due to accounting reasons. The total package for RB Leipzig will amount to €30m, including bonuses. Gruda will then get a contract until 2031, which has already been agreed.

“Bayern have always had him on their list, even before his move to Brighton. However, he is currently not a concrete transfer target for Bayern – unless something extraordinary happens, such as the sale of Michael Olise.”

Gruda seems to prefer living and playing his football in Germany and whether he even considers moving back to Brighton remains to be seen. The Seagulls - who are flying high in the Premier League - also have a number of options on the right flank.

Minteh - who almost joined Liverpool last summer - is just returning from injury, while Paraguayan international Diego Gomez has also excelled in the wide right position this term.

Zadok Yohanna, Femi Azeez, Malick Yalcouye are all available, while the likes of Amario Cozier-Duberry and Harry Howell are out on loan.

Gruda's form is impressive but whether he returns to the Premier League with Brighton anytime soon is debatable. Attention will now likely turn to maximising their fee.

#1944. Japan vs Paraguay - prediction, team news, lineups

By Ben Sully | 16 Nov 2026 00:29, Last updated: 17 Nov 2026 18:00

Japan and Paraguay will conclude their respective 2026 schedules when they face off in Tuesday's friendly in Singapore.

The Samurai Blue pulled off a thrilling win over Brazil last time out, while Paraguay cruised to a commanding victory over Singapore in their most recent outing.

Japan head into Tuesday's fixture in fine form, having lost just one of their previous 16 internationals.

Their only defeat in that period came in the Round of 32 tie against Brazil at the 2026 World Cup, which saw them spurn a leading position in a narrow 2-1 defeat.

After conceding a late winner in that contest, Hajime Moriyasu's side managed to exact an element of revenge with a stoppage-time winner of their own in Saturday's friendly against Brazil.

The Samurai Blue looked to have wasted another strong position after Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura saw their efforts cancelled out by a Vinicius Junior brace, before Coventry City's Tatsuhiro Sakamoto turned the game back in Japan's favour with a 91st-minute goal.

Sakamoto's effort made it two wins in Japan's last three head-to-head meetings with Brazil, while making it five games without defeat since their World Cup elimination.

Japan should fancy their chances of extending their unbeaten run with a win, having won four of their previous five meetings with Paraguay (D1) since losing on penalties in the last 16 of the 2010 World Cup.

After eventually being eliminated in the quarter-finals in 2010, Paraguay had to wait 16 years until their next appearance in football's biggest tournament.

La Albirroja certainly made an impact at the 2026 World Cup, advancing to the knockout rounds before eliminating Germany on penalties in the Round of 32.

However, their run ultimately came to an end in a feisty last-16 clash against France, with Kylian Mbappe's 70th-minute penalty proving decisive as Paraguay fell to a narrow 1-0 loss.

Gustavo Alfaro's side have since made a positive return to action with three consecutive wins against Bolivia, Colombia and Singapore.

Gustavo Caballero netted a brace as Paraguay cruised to a 4-1 success in their most recent outing against Singapore, representing just the third time La Albirroja have scored two or more goals in 2026.

Their strength has ultimately been at the opposite end of the pitch, having conceded more than one goal in just two of their 11 games in the current calendar year.

Japan have announced that Daichi Kamada has been allowed to return to Crystal Palace after playing 72 minutes in the win over Brazil.

Ko Itakura, Yukinari Sugawara and Kaishu Sano are among those who could start if Moriyasu opts to rotate his side.

Sakamoto, Takumi Minamino and Koki Ogawa could come in to freshen up Japan's attack for Tuesday's friendly.

As for Paraguay, Alfaro is expected to make wholesale changes after naming an experimental XI for the win over Singapore.

Juan Jose Caceres, Gustavo Gomez and Omar Alderete are likely to come into the back four for Paraguay's final outing of 2026.

Diego Gomez, Miguel Almiron and Julio Enciso are also among those who are expected to start against Japan.

Suzuki; Sugawara, Seko, Itakura, Ito; Ka Sano, Tanaka; Sakamoto, Minamino, Nakamura; Ogawa

Gill; Caceres, G. Gomez, Alderete, Maidana; Cuenca, Galarza, D. Gomez, Almiron; Benitez, Enciso

Japan will be full of confidence after pulling off a notable win over Brazil, and while we think they will claim another victory on Tuesday, we believe the scoreline will be close against a Paraguay team that is usually a tough side to break down.

#1943. Messi was a deity among Argentina’s unholy rabble

Little sorcerer calls time on playing for his country six weeks after World Cup final defeat which was marred by brutality of his team-mates

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Lionel Messi’s haunted expression told you more than a three-page retirement statement, artfully displayed alongside a golden pen, ever could. Sobbing and desolate under a cloudless New Jersey sky, he understood that his last game for Argentina had also been among his worst.

Where four years earlier he had adorned the greatest World Cup final with two goals, he found no artistry to salvage this abomination of an encore, drifting into anonymity while his team-mates triggered a bare-knuckle brawl. No wonder he stood apart while Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina did their worst, preferring to absorb one more chorus of adoration from the blue-and-white disciples before forsaking the stage for good.

You could make the case that Messi, as captain of an unholy rabble that had sought only to kick lumps out of Spain, should have taken a moral lead by hauling his team-mates into line, rather than reducing himself to their level by agitating to have Marc Cucurella sent off.

And yet for 20 years, the little sorcerer stayed aloof from his nation’s most lurid antics on the pitch, establishing himself as a strangely beatific presence on whom the highest ideals could be projected. Anybody who has heard Messi’s name being chanted by 50,000 fervent Argentines would have felt it. He was as close as 21st-century sport has come to a secular deity, the object of such veneration that Pope Francis felt compelled to remind Catholics that it was sacrilegious to keep calling him God.

Today, with one agonised announcement, that glorious delirium is over, and already Argentina seems not to know what to do with itself. Pablo Giralt, a sports anchor in Buenos Aires, was unable even to speak when he heard the news live on air, while shattered young fans described how they had called their parents in tears.

Everybody had known the moment was approaching, given the finality of his exit from the final and the subsequent death of his father, Jorge, but it still triggered an unbearable sense of loss.

Messi was the force who galvanised a nation, propelling his side from the unfathomable low of defeat to Saudi Arabia at the 2022 World Cup to holding the trophy aloft 26 days later. Who could ever hope to emulate him, to detonate such joy that the team’s homecoming bus parade in the capital had to be abandoned for a helicopter ride because of the millions on the streets?

“Thank you, God, for making me Argentine,” Messi wrote in his earnest sign-off, his strength of allegiance unfailing to the end. As a veteran of 207 international matches, with his last at La Bombonera distinguished by an ecstatic ovation, he understood both the passions he unleashed among his people and the extent to which his own story became that of an entire country.

You struggled to imagine what life was like in the eye of this madness, with his every move stalked. For the wonder of Messi was that the cult went beyond borders, that the joy he inspired across six World Cups made him beloved to billions. An abiding memory of the 2022 final is of the walk back to the metro station in Doha, where thousands of Nepalese and Bangladeshi supporters, all part of the vast migrant workforce that had built the stadiums, united in “Messi, Messi” refrains even at 1am.

Messi was majestic at that tournament, so imperious in filleting Croatia in the semi-finals that Argentina’s TV reporters abandoned even the pretence of objectivity. “Truly, you made your mark in everyone’s life, and that to me is beyond winning any World Cup,” gushed Sofia Martinez of Television Publica. And when he won it all, the mark only deepened. To occupy any press box at the World Cup where Argentina were involved this summer was to see South American colleagues in “Messi 10” jerseys, helplessly in thrall to his greatness.

As a 39-year-old, he confounded every expectation, scoring a hat-trick against Algeria and breaking Miroslav Klose’s World Cup goals record. Even when engineering those implausible fightbacks against Egypt and England, he held a volatile team together with a minimum of fuss.

Lionel Messi: #FIFAWorldCup edition 🇦🇷🌟 pic.twitter.com/E2xOh3Iose

To study Messi at his last World Cup was to see a man spared the obligation to do anything off the ball. For large periods of each game, the most minutely scrutinised athlete on the planet would do little besides wander around, only to ignite when it mattered most. You saw it in the fateful semi-final with England, where, at 1-0 down, he sloped off to the right touchline as if absent-mindedly gardening. Except he was plotting his opponents’ downfall, working out the precise spots from which to unleash two sumptuous crosses and shatter English hearts.

That alchemy would elude him in the final, where Argentina’s bid for immortality brought only instant notoriety, not to mention £236,000 in fines for misconduct. Was Messi’s image hurt by his connection to the chaos? Not in the long run. Nobody likes to cling to the fact that Pelé’s swansong for Brazil was a drawn friendly with Yugoslavia, or that Diego Maradona bowed out of World Cup football by failing a drug test for ephedrine. What endure are the indelible masterpieces those players bequeathed en route.

It will be the same for Messi, a genius defined less by his ending than by the electrifying adrenalin rush he produced along the way, spanning three finals, 21 goals, and countless flourishes to take the breath away. “Thank you” was all he had left to say. And yet the gratitude, ultimately, is all ours.
